channel.title: Keeping up with Agents
channel.description: AI moves fast. Keep up. AI-narrated deep dives that navigate the field's live arguments, built from verified wikis of major AI events' talks: who is on each side of every real disagreement, the variable that explains the split, and what a technical product manager would do about it. From Clay Waters. First season: the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 (231 talks, almost a million words). Hosts are AI-generated; every underlying quote is verified verbatim against the source video.
channel.itunes:author: Clay Waters

item.title: Your Model Is Swappable. Your Harness Is Not.
item.description:
The people building the most advanced AI systems plan on switching their primary tool (their harness: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Claude Cowork) within about a year. This episode is about what follows you when you do. The industry made the model swappable; nobody made the harness swappable, and the harness is where your skills, your MCP connections, and your assistant's memory of you accumulate. From the most discussed topic at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026: the log lock-in warning, the Skyrim save-file analogy, and the habit that makes switching a non-event: keep your AI assets as files you own, and keep your own test cases. The skill is the compiled binary; the eval is the source code. If you switched tools tomorrow, what would follow you?
Disclosure: this episode's hosts are AI-generated (via Google NotebookLM) from the underlying wiki and written analysis. Sources, transcripts, and the full corpus behind every claim are at https://github.com/claywaters13/keeping-up-with-agents.

item.title: Zero Settled: What 231 AI Engineer World's Fair Talks Actually Disagree On
item.description:
We ran 231 talks from the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 through a maturity rubric — settled, consolidating, contested, or frontier — and got a surprise: not one of the 134 recurring concepts came back settled. 87 are consolidating, 43 are actively contested, and 4 are frontier. This episode walks the sharpest fault lines practitioners are actually split on right now: deterministic verification versus LLM-as-a-judge, whether human approval gates are real control or theater, and compaction versus append-only context logs, including the two frontier labs quietly taking opposite sides. The keep-up message: the field isn't a syllabus you finish, it's a set of live arguments, and the fastest way to track them is asking an assistant that has actually read all 231 talks.
Disclosure: this episode's hosts are AI-generated (via Google NotebookLM) from the underlying wiki and written analysis. Sources, transcripts, and the full corpus behind every claim are at https://github.com/claywaters13/aiewf-2026-wiki.
